text: These include namely renewable diesel and biodiesel, with bio-crude and bio-oil also being investigated. Liquefied RNG, referred to in the maritime industry as bio-liquefied natural gas, is also considered a drop-in substitute for liquefied natural gas within the existing natural gas fleet. Emerging non-drop-in fuels include bio-methanol and lignin-alcohol mixes. Additional non- biofuels being investigated include other varieties of methanol (namely e-methanol), ammonia, and hydrogen. Presently, most U.S. ports are not equipped to supply alternative fuels like biofuels, and a readily available supply chain is still developing (DOE 2024b). Significant progress has been made in the bunkering and use of marine biofuels through various trails and voyages, demonstrating the viability of biofuels in the maritime sector. In the United States, renewable diesel, biodiesel, and bio-liquefied natural gas have seen successful deployment (Maritime Logistics Professionals 2021; Diesel Direct 2025; Kosmajac 2025; Scania 2025). Additionally, Oak Ridge National Laboratory is actively testing the use of advanced biofuels such as fast pyrolysis and hydrothermal liquefaction biointermediates in marine engines, with preparations to move from laboratory testing to sea trials by 2027 (Bioenergy Technologies Office 2024). Internationally, successful trials and voyages using B100, renewable diesel, bio- methanol, and bio-liquefied natural gas further illustrate biofuel momentum within the maritime industry. While current biofuel prices are generally higher than fossil marine fuels (e.g., $967–$1,157 per metric ton for biofuels compared to $700 for marine gas oil in 2019), they are projected to decrease by 36%–43% between 2022 and 2040. Strategies to lower costs include utilizing waste feedstocks, improving logistics, coprocessing with fossil fuels, and developing high-value coproducts (DOE 2024b).In 2023, biofuels accounted for 6.1% of Union Pacific’s fuel use (Luczak 2024). There are five major types of biopower generation technologies: combustion, co-firing, gasification, anaerobic digestion, and pyrolysis. Combustion is used by most biopower plants today— bioenergy feedstock is burned directly to produce steam that turns an electricity-generating turbine (International Renewable Energy Agency 2012). The steam could also be used for industrial processes or to heat buildings in combined heat and power facilities. Co-firing power plants substitute solid biomass for a portion of the other primary fuel in use. In gasification systems, solid biomass is heated in a restricted supply of air to produce an energy-rich gas that can fuel steam generators, combustion turbines, combined-cycle technologies, or fuel cells. Anaerobic digestion is a biological process in which microorganisms break down biodegradable material in the absence of oxygen.
